newsitem.title: USA: Study sees rise in U.S. natgas imports from Canada.
newsitem.headline: Study sees rise in U.S. natgas imports from Canada.

text.p: U.S. imports of natural gas from Canada could increase to between 3.6 and 4.9 trillion cubic feet by 2005 from 2.8 Tcf in 1996, according to a study released Wednesday by a U.S. gas industry organization.

The study released by the INGAA Foundation on the North American gas market also said Mexico will mainly be an export market for the next decade, with northern Mexico ripe for increasing gas demand because of growth in its domestic and export industries.

The study, prepared by the Brattle Group of Cambridge, Massachusetts, found a trend toward producer- and marketer-supported investments in capacity and a trend toward smaller, incremental expansion intended to match the pace of market growth.

While the report predicted that U.S. imports of Canadian gas will continue to grow, it said the expansion should be done cautiously because both the Canadian and U.S. gas industries need to avoid capacity gluts and resulting boom and bust production cycles.
Because of the continuing integration of the U.S. and Canadian natural gas markets, the report said it will become easier to add pipeline import capacity.
The study considered three market scenarios that cover the U.S. regions where Canadian gas flows -- the West, the Midwest and the Northeast.

In the scenario for a relatively stable market, total Canadian import requirements are 3.2 Tcf in 2000 and 3.6 Tcf in 2005. In this outlook, there would be little, if any, displacement of U.S. domestic gas by Canadian supplies.
Another scenario assumed much higher Canadian imports, equal to 175 percent of the growth in the Midwest and Northeast, and 58 percent demand growth in the West.

This is consistent with growth seen in the last series of pipeline expansions to the West from Canada, and from growth suggested if just one or two of the larger currently proposed import pipelines are built, the study said.
Under this scenario, imports from Canada grow to 3.8 Tcf by 2000 and to 4.9 Tcf by 2005, and U.S. domestic gas has significant displacement.
The third scenario also put imports of Canadian gas at 3.8 Tcf by 2000 and 4.9 Tcf by 2005, but it predicted higher overall U.S. demand for gas, largely for electric power generation.
Even with increased demand, the report said Canadian gas would displace U.S. sources of gas supply in the Midwest and Northeast.
